name: Photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT)

lead: ALA-PDT applies aminolevulinic acid to the skin and then shines light on it, which kills targeted cells. People with severe or stubborn acne pursue it to target oil glands and inflamed lesions for clearer skin, sometimes on the body too.

Cells accumulate protoporphyrin IX, which produces reactive oxygen species on light exposure and damages the treated cells. It is established for actinic keratosis and some skin cancers. For acne, a 2016 review called it safe and effective, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue or violet light alone, so results are mixed.

paras: It is a clinician-administered treatment: the drug is applied, left for a set period, then the area is exposed to light. Courses are typically sessions in a clinic.
Marked redness, moderate to severe pain, burning and photosensitivity are commonly reported. It is performed by clinicians.

chain: Light activates photosensitizer in oil glands
angle.text: Light activates a photosensitizer in oil glands and inflamed lesions, reducing inflammatory acne for clearer skin. Some trials and a review report benefit for acne, with mixed results.

lead: ALA-PDT is a clinic procedure in which a dermatologist applies aminolevulinic acid (ALA) to the skin and then shines a light of a matching wavelength on it. Cells in the treated area turn ALA into a light-sensitive compound, protoporphyrin IX, and the light then triggers reactive oxygen species that destroy the targeted cells.[1][2] People look into it for visible skin concerns: inflamed, stubborn or severe acne, sun-damaged skin with rough sun spots (actinic keratoses), and, off label, general facial rejuvenation.[2][3]

Because the effect is confined to the area that is both sensitised and illuminated, the treatment can be directed at the face, and the skin typically clears and renews after the sunburn-like reaction settles, usually over several weeks.[2] DermNet lists acne and facial rejuvenation among the off-label or investigational uses, while actinic keratosis, Bowen disease and superficial basal cell carcinoma are the approved ones.[2]

For acne, a 2016 systematic review described PDT as a safe and effective treatment, while one phase II trial found improvement that was not better than blue or violet light alone.[1] A small randomized trial compared ALA with its methyl ester (MAL) for inflamed facial acne.[4] A 2022 network meta-analysis of acne treatments covered physical treatments, including light-based ones, alongside drugs.[5] Redness, burning, pain and light sensitivity for about a day are the main reported side effects.[1][2]

paras: A photosensitizer collects in the target tissue and is activated by light, passing energy to oxygen and producing singlet oxygen and other reactive species that damage cell membranes and proteins; because damage occurs only where light is applied, the effect stays localised.[1] ALA is a prodrug: it is the first compound in the body's heme-making pathway, and applying extra of it makes protoporphyrin IX accumulate faster than cells convert it to heme.[6] The compound peaks within hours and clears in about a day, which limits how long skin stays light-sensitive.[1]
In acne, proposed mechanisms include damage to the oil-producing sebaceous glands and to acne-associated bacteria, though the details are still being studied.[5]

According to DermNet, the skin may be lightly scraped or needled to help the drug penetrate, the photosensitiser is left on for about 3 to 6 hours, and the area is then illuminated with laser or non-laser light or with daylight. Artificial-light sessions usually last 5 to 45 minutes, daylight sessions about 2 hours, and a second session may be given 7 to 10 days later.[2] A local anaesthetic spray can ease discomfort, and the area is covered afterwards to block further light.[2]
Treated skin develops a sunburn-like reaction, with the surface typically healing within 4 to 8 weeks.[2]

PDT has been studied mainly for severe or inflammatory acne. Early trial results suggested a benefit in severe cases, and a 2016 systematic review called it safe and effective.[1] In the trial that compared ALA-PDT with MAL-PDT, 15 patients with at least 12 inflamed facial lesions were treated and followed for treatment effect and tolerability.[4]

Actinic keratoses are rough, scaly sun-damage patches, and ALA-PDT is an approved treatment for them. Facial rejuvenation is listed as an off-label use.[2] A 2025 phase 1 registration studied activating an ALA product with a broadband light device for actinic keratoses and photodamage.[7]

Around 1900, Oscar Raab and Hermann von Tappeiner found that light and oxygen were needed for dyes to kill cells, and von Tappeiner named the effect photodynamic action.[1] In 1978 Thomas Dougherty's group reported treating 113 skin and subcutaneous tumours, with total or partial resolution in 111, and Photofrin became the first PDT agent approved for clinical use, in Canada in 1993.[1] Topical ALA-based PDT for skin conditions developed from this work.[8]

The main side effect is skin photosensitivity, which for ALA lasts about 24 hours.[1][2] DermNet lists stinging or burning, redness, swelling, itching, crusting, peeling and blistering, and rarely skin infection; a loss of pigment can occur and may be permanent.[2] In acne treatment, marked redness and moderate to severe pain or burning have been reported.[1]

A randomized, investigator-blinded trial of 15 patients with inflamed facial acne compared ALA-PDT with MAL-PDT for effect and tolerability.[4] A 2016 systematic review called PDT safe and effective for acne, while a phase II trial found it no better than blue or violet light alone.[1]

A network meta-analysis of randomized trials in acne vulgaris compared topical, oral, physical and combined treatments in mild-to-moderate and moderate-to-severe acne.[5] A 2001 open study examined ALA-PDT for large or multiple patches of Bowen disease and basal cell carcinoma, and a 2004 review covered laser and PDT for non-melanoma skin cancer; these concern skin cancer rather than appearance.[8][9] Registered trials cover actinic keratosis, including a phase 3 field-treatment study and daylight-PDT studies.[10][11]

timeline.event: Raab and von Tappeiner describe photodynamic action.[1]
Dougherty's group reports PDT results in 113 skin and subcutaneous tumours.[1]
Photofrin becomes the first approved PDT agent.[1]
Randomized trial compares ALA-PDT and MAL-PDT for acne.[4]
A systematic review calls PDT safe and effective for acne.[1]
